sections.title: The Mitzva of Birkat Ha-mazon
sections.html:
It is a Torah commandment that after a person eats bread and is satisfied, he must bless God, as it is stated (Devarim 8:10): "You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God for the good land that He has given you." The Sages learned that Birkat Ha-mazon must include three matters: from the words "and you shall bless the Lord your God," they learned that one must recite the blessing of Ha-zan, in which we bless God for the food. From the words "for the land," they learned that one must bless and give thanks for the land. And from the fact that the Torah went on to say "for the good land that He has given you," they learned that one must bless for what is good and choicest in the land, namely Jerusalem (Berakhot 48b).

The Torah commandment is that the one reciting the blessing mention these matters in any wording he wishes, according to his understanding and his power of expression. Then Moshe, Yehoshua, David and Shlomo came and instituted a choice and complete wording, according to the good that had been added in their days. When the manna came down for Israel, Moshe Rabbeinu instituted the wording of the blessing of Ha-zan, and no wording had yet been fixed for the blessing over the good land. When Israel entered the Land, Yehoshua bin Nun instituted the wording of the blessing of the land, and no wording had yet been fixed for the blessing over the good and choicest place in the land. When King David established Jerusalem as the city of holiness and of the kingdom, he instituted the wording of the blessing "for Israel Your people and for Jerusalem Your city," and when King Shlomo built the Holy Temple, he added "for the great and holy House." While the Temple stood, they would ask that God continue its existence, and after it was destroyed, they instituted a wording in which we ask God to have mercy on us, to build Jerusalem, to restore the kingship of the House of David to its place and to build the Temple (Berakhot 48b; Rashba; Ramban, as cited in BY 187:1; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 187:1-3).

The Sages said (Berakhot 48b; SA 187:2-3) that it is obligatory to mention in the blessing of the land the praise of the land, that it is a desirable, good and spacious land. One must also mention the covenant of circumcision (brit mila) and the Torah, because it is through these two mitzvot that we inherit the land. As was said to Avraham Avinu when he was commanded regarding the covenant of circumcision (Bereishit 17:7-8): "I will establish My covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you throughout their generations as an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your descendants after you. And I will give to you and to your descendants after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession, and I will be their God."

We have likewise learned that it is by virtue of the Torah and the mitzvot that we inherit the land, as it is stated at the beginning of the passage in which we were commanded regarding Birkat Ha-mazon (Devarim 8:1): "All the commandment that I command you this day you shall observe to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and inherit the land that the Lord swore to your fathers." And it is also stated (Tehillim 105:44-45): "He gave them the lands of the nations, and they inherited the toil of peoples, so that they might keep His statutes and observe His teachings. Halleluya."

The Sages further said that the mention of the covenant must precede the mention of the Torah, because in connection with the covenant of circumcision thirteen covenants are mentioned, whereas over the Torah only three covenants were made. The covenant of circumcision expresses the intrinsic holiness with which God sanctified His people Israel, a holiness that does not depend on our choice, and it is the foundation for receiving the Torah, which demands of us that we choose the good.

In the third blessing they instituted mentioning the kingship of the House of David, because it was through David that Jerusalem was sanctified, and the essential settlement of the land and of Jerusalem depends on the kingship of Israel (Berakhot 48b; SA 188:3).

sections.title: The Blessing of Ha-tov Ve-hametiv
sections.html:
After the destruction of the Temple and the devastation of the land, it seemed as though there was no longer any hope for the rebuilding of the land and of Jerusalem, and no longer any point in continuing to bless God "for the good land." Therefore they added and instituted the blessing of Ha-tov Ve-hametiv ("who is good and does good"), in order to strengthen the faith that everything is for the good, and that even the destruction, the exile and the suffering are meant to rectify us and to bring us anew to a more complete rebuilding of the land, Jerusalem and the Temple.

The Sages in Yavne instituted the blessing on a special day, the day on which those killed at Beitar were given over for burial. Beitar was a large city in Judea, and it was the capital of Bar Kokhba, and from it they hoped to restore Israel's independence and the building of the Temple. When it fell and was destroyed, the horn of Israel was cut down and the troubles grew very great, and the wicked kingdom decreed that Jerusalem be plowed over and that the names of the land and of Jerusalem be changed, in order to wipe out their memory from the world. They further decreed that those killed at Beitar not be buried. Some time later, when a new king was appointed, permission was given to bury the slain, and it was found that a miracle had been done for them and they had not decomposed. The Sages said (Berakhot 48b): "On the day that those killed at Beitar were given over for burial, they instituted Ha-tov Ve-hametiv in Yavne. 'Ha-tov' (who is good) – that they did not decompose; and 'Ve-hametiv' (and does good) – that they were given over for burial." Our master Rav Kook explained (Ein Aya there) that from the fact that they did not decompose we learn that the destruction and the exile did not nullify the essential selfhood of Israel. And in the fact that they were given over for burial there is a hint of the promise that they will yet rise to their destiny at the end of days, and this is a sign of the fulfillment of all the prophets' promises of revival and redemption.

Since the obligation to recite it is different – the first three blessings being from the Torah while this one is rabbinic – therefore, upon completing the first three blessings, the one reciting the blessing answers "Amen" after his own blessing: "who builds Jerusalem [in His mercy] – Amen" (SA 188:1).

And since the series of Torah blessings concludes at the end of the third blessing, the fourth blessing, which the Sages instituted, is a blessing in its own right, and therefore it opens with "Barukh" ("Blessed"). For this is the rule: when a blessing is adjacent to another, it relies on it and does not need to open with "Barukh"; but when it is a blessing that stands on its own, it must open with "Barukh."1

The Sages further said (Berakhot 46a) that the guest should bless the host after Birkat Ha-mazon, and this is the wording of the blessing (SA 201:1): "May it be His will that this host not be shamed or disgraced, neither in this world nor in the World to Come; may he succeed in all his dealings, and may his possessions be successful and close to the city; may Satan have no power over the work of his hands, and may no matter of sin or thought of iniquity come before him, from now and forever." One may lengthen and expand this wording, and this is the practice of those of Sephardic descent. Many of those of Ashkenazic descent are accustomed to make do with a short wording: "May the Merciful One bless the master of this house." But ideally it is proper to say the wording whose basis is in the Gemara (MB 201:5; and below 5:4).

Since we have already merited to be sanctified through the mitzva of Birkat Ha-mazon, Israel has been accustomed to add personal requests that open with "Ha-raḥaman" ("May the Merciful One"), as well as other general prayers for the redemption. And although this is not an enactment of the Sages, since this has been the practice since the days of the Rishonim, the custom is binding, each community according to its custom. However, if a person needs to interrupt by speaking or to go somewhere, since he has finished the fourth blessing he may interrupt, and afterward, when he is able, he should complete what he omitted (see below, note 13).

sections.title: The Meaning of the Blessing of Ha-zan
sections.html:
In order to delve into the subject of Birkat Ha-mazon, one must contemplate the entire passage at whose center we were commanded regarding Birkat Ha-mazon (Devarim 8:1-18). The first verse presents the general aim: "All the commandment that I command you this day you shall observe to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and inherit the land that the Lord swore to your fathers." Afterward two central foundations are explained: the first, that God feeds everything, as we say in the first blessing; the second, the praise of the Land of Israel, as we say in the second and third blessings. We will focus first on the foundations connected to the first blessing, the blessing of Ha-zan ("who feeds").

Many times, when a person's livelihood is readily available to him, he forgets that God watches over him and provides for him, and therefore the Torah instructed (ibid. 8:2): "You shall remember all the way that the Lord your God led you these forty years in the wilderness, in order to afflict you, to test you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep His commandments or not." Life in the wilderness was hard; out of the many hardships one could rail against Heaven, and on the other hand, one could strengthen oneself in faith and contemplate the miracles through which the Holy One, blessed be He, sustains Israel. The most difficult test was connected to eating the manna. A person is accustomed to worry about tomorrow; for this purpose he prepares his food for himself through his work in the field, in industry and in commerce. But all this was not possible in the wilderness. It was forbidden even to keep manna from one day to the next, and it was not even possible to eat more than a person needed, for the amount of manna was limited to what a person needed to eat in one day and no more. Every Jew had to believe in God that tomorrow too He would send down manna for him from heaven. And whoever weakened in his faith felt hunger, as it is stated (ibid. 3-4): "He afflicted you and let you hunger, and fed you the manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know."

Through this test it was engraved in our national consciousness that nature does not exist by itself, but rather God is the one who provides for everything – "in order to make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that comes out of the mouth of the Lord does man live. Your clothing did not wear out upon you, nor did your foot swell, these forty years." These were the first forty years of the appearance of the people of Israel in the world, years in which it learned and internalized the values of the Torah. Through the miraculous life in the wilderness we learned well that everything comes from God in order to do good for us, and even if He withholds His blessing from us for a certain period, this is only out of His love for us, in order to set us on the path of truth, as it is stated (ibid. 5-6): "You shall know in your heart that just as a man disciplines his son, so the Lord your God disciplines you. And you shall keep the commandments of the Lord your God, to walk in His ways and to fear Him."

The essence of the mitzva is to bless God when a person has eaten and is satisfied, as it is stated (Devarim 8:10): "You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God for the good land that He has given you." For when a person is satiated he is liable to become arrogant and forget that everything comes from God, and about this the Torah goes on to warn (ibid. 11-16): "Beware lest you forget the Lord your God by not keeping His commandments, His ordinances and His statutes, which I command you this day; lest you eat and be satisfied, and build good houses and dwell in them; and your herds and your flocks multiply, and your silver and gold multiply, and all that you have multiply; and your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage; who led you through the great and terrible wilderness, of fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty ground where there was no water; who brought forth water for you out of the flinty rock; who fed you in the wilderness with manna, which your fathers did not know, in order to afflict you and in order to test you, to do you good in your end."

sections.title: The Centrality of the Blessing of the Land
sections.html:
The second foundation that runs through the entire passage of Birkat Ha-mazon is the praise of the Land of Israel. The Sages said (Bamidbar Rabba 23:7) about the blessings in Birkat Ha-mazon: "None of them is more beloved than the blessing 'for the land.'" And this is the plain meaning of the verse, that the main aim is to bless God for the good land, as it is stated (Devarim 8:10): "You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God for the good land that He has given you." The third blessing, over Jerusalem, is also a continuation of the blessing of the land, for Jerusalem is the heart of "the good land." We likewise learned from the verse that opens the passage that the main fulfillment of the mitzvot is specifically in the Land of Israel, as it is stated (Devarim 8:1): "All the commandment that I command you this day you shall observe to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and inherit the land that the Lord swore to your fathers."

The explanation for this is that the main purpose of Israel is to reveal the word of God in the world while grappling with the complications of earthly life. Therefore the situation in which we are fed by manna that came down from heaven is temporary, in order to acquire the basic awareness that God is the one who feeds everything. But the aim is that man be a partner with the Holy One, blessed be He, in perfecting the world, by bringing forth his food from the earth through plowing, sowing, planting and raising animals. Through this he will reveal the Divine image within him, bring out the good in earthliness, and rise to a connection full of life with God. Indeed, the manna that came down from heaven had no waste, and it was entirely absorbed into the limbs, without their needing to relieve themselves after eating it. But man's main destiny is to eat physical foods, which contain waste, yet on the other hand the good in them is more beloved, and holier sparks are hidden within them. For this purpose we were given the Land of Israel, which is the Holy Land; although it is a physical land, it is holy, and the fruits that grow in it are holy.

Many tend to think that the further a person distances himself from physicality and from sensing the various tastes in foods, the purer and holier he will be. But the Torah teaches us that in the Land of Israel there is great value to physical abundance, to varied food and its excellent taste, which too was created by the Holy One, blessed be He, in order to bring us to our completeness. Therefore the Torah takes the trouble to praise before us the goodness and desirability of the Land of Israel, as it is stated (ibid. 7-9): "For the Lord your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of springs and depths flowing forth in valley and hill; a land of wheat and barley, and vine and fig and pomegranate; a land of olive oil and honey; a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity, you will lack nothing in it; a land whose stones are iron and from whose hills you will dig copper." And therefore we were commanded to bless God for this, as it is stated (Devarim 8:10): "You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God for the good land that He has given you."

In the first blessing we dwell on the foundation that God is the one "who feeds all," and just as He gave us the manna in the wilderness miraculously, so He always sustains nature; thus, the root of all the food we eat is from Him, may He be blessed, alone. In the second blessing we bless God for granting us the ability to be partners in perfecting the world and in bringing forth food from the earth, and therefore the blessing concludes: "for the land and for the food."2

However, there is a concern lest success in building the land drown a person in desire and arrogance and make him forget his destiny. And about this we were commanded (Devarim 8:11-18): "Beware lest you forget the Lord your God by not keeping His commandments, His ordinances and His statutes, which I command you this day; lest you eat and be satisfied, and build good houses and dwell in them; and your herds and your flocks multiply, and your silver and gold multiply, and all that you have multiply; and your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord your God … and you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' But you shall remember the Lord your God, for it is He who gives you power to get wealth, in order to establish His covenant which He swore to your fathers, as it is this day."

In Birkat Ha-mazon we remind ourselves again that God is the one who gave us the food and the land, and through this we will be roused to understand that the strength, the satisfaction and the joy that we received from the food are meant to sanctify us and to elevate us.

sections.title: Laws of Reciting Birkat Ha-mazon and Educating Children
sections.html:
The one reciting the blessing must make audible to his own ear what he utters with his mouth, and if he did not articulate the words with his lips, he has not fulfilled his obligation. Ideally, one should say the blessing aloud, because the voice arouses concentration. One who does not understand Hebrew may say the blessing in translation into a language he understands (SA 185:1-3; MB 1-3; and above 1:6-7).

After the fact, one who omitted passages from Birkat Ha-mazon has fulfilled his obligation, as long as he mentioned the foundations that must be in Birkat Ha-mazon. These are the foundations: to bless God for the food, and within the blessing to mention His name and that He is King of the universe (SA 187:1; MB 4); in the second blessing, to thank God for the land, to mention that it is desirable, good and spacious, and to mention the covenant of circumcision and the study of Torah; in the third blessing, to mention Jerusalem, the Temple and the kingship of the House of David; and in the fourth blessing, to say its essence.

A child who has reached the age of education (ḥinukh), that is, the age at which he understands in a general way the matter of blessings, it is a mitzva to train him to recite all the blessings, and foremost among them Birkat Ha-mazon, which is the most important of the blessings. Most children reach the age of education at around six. Before that, when they understand a little of how to bless, it is good to begin teaching them to bless, but they are not yet obligated to bless. Even children who have already reached the age of education, when it is hard for them to recite all of Birkat Ha-mazon, should be accustomed to say the first blessing, and in this way they will progress according to their ability.3

sections.title: The Torah Obligation When Satisfied, and the Rabbinic Obligation for a Kezayit
sections.html:
By Torah law a person is obligated to recite Birkat Ha-mazon when he has eaten a meal with bread and is satisfied, as it is stated (Devarim 8:10): "You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless." The Sages added and instituted that even a person who ate a kezayit of bread, since he derived enjoyment, should recite all of Birkat Ha-mazon. The Sages said (Berakhot 20b) that the ministering angels argued before the Holy One, blessed be He: "Master of the Universe, it is written in Your Torah (Devarim 10:19): 'who shows no favor and takes no bribe,' yet do You not show favor to Israel, as it is stated (Bamidbar 6:26): 'May the Lord lift up His countenance toward you'? He said to them: And shall I not show favor to Israel? For I wrote for them in the Torah: 'You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God,' and they are exacting with themselves and bless even for a kezayit."

When a person is in doubt whether he recited Birkat Ha-mazon for what he ate: if he was satisfied, since the doubt concerns a Torah commandment, he must be stringent and recite Birkat Ha-mazon. If he was not satisfied, since the doubt concerns a rabbinic commandment, he should not bless (SA 184:4).

If his friend remembers seeing him bless, he may rely on him (Maharsham 4:29). Likewise, if he himself knows that he is accustomed to bless immediately after eating, even though he does not remember it precisely, he may rely on the presumption (ḥazaka) that he presumably blessed (based on Halakhot Ketanot 2:278; see Kaf Ha-ḥayim 184:21).

According to most poskim, even if he ate only a kezayit of bread, if he ate other foods as well and from all of them together he became satisfied, he is obligated to recite Birkat Ha-mazon by Torah law.4

Of course women too are obligated in Birkat Ha-mazon, but a doubt arose whether their obligation is from the Torah or rabbinic, for perhaps, as in several matters, there is a difference between men and women: with men the emphasis is more on obligation, whereas with women the emphasis is more on volunteering. Indeed, the entire doubt concerns only the question of whether women are obligated in Birkat Ha-mazon by Torah law, but by rabbinic law it is clear that women are obligated like men (SA 186:1; MB 187:9).5

sections.title: Additions on Shabbat and Festivals
sections.html:
On holy days on which a Musaf offering was brought, the Sages instituted mentioning the holiness of the day in Birkat Ha-mazon, for eating on these days is not like eating on weekdays; rather, it carries an added measure of mitzva and holiness, and this must be expressed in the blessing. On Shabbat one says "Retzei Ve-haḥalitzenu"; and on Yom Tov, Ḥol Ha-mo'ed and Rosh Ḥodesh one says "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo." They instituted saying the addition in the blessing of Boneh Yerushalayim ("who builds Jerusalem"), because it contains a plea for mercy, and the mention that the Sages instituted also contains a plea for mercy. In "Retzei Ve-haḥalitzenu" we ask that we merit the holiness of the Shabbat day, to cease from labor and rest on it, and to see the consolation of Zion and Jerusalem. And in "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" we ask that God remember us for good, have mercy on us and save us (Berakhot 49a; Shabbat 24a, and Tosafot there).

When Yom Tov or Rosh Ḥodesh falls on Shabbat, one first says "Retzei Ve-haḥalitzenu," because Shabbat is more frequent and holier, and afterward one says "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" (SA 188:5; MB 13).

On Ḥanukka and Purim, on which the Sages instituted giving thanks for the miracle, one adds the "Al Ha-nissim" wording in the blessing of the land, which is a blessing of thanksgiving.

One who began eating Se'uda Shlishit (the third Shabbat meal) before sunset and finished it after the emergence of the stars says "Retzei Ve-haḥalitzenu" in Birkat Ha-mazon. For since he began eating on Shabbat, he already became obligated in Birkat Ha-mazon on Shabbat, and consequently became obligated to mention "Retzei Ve-haḥalitzenu" in it. The same law applies on other days: if one began the meal at a time when something had to be added in Birkat Ha-mazon, even though he finished his meal after the emergence of the stars, he must add and mention what he was already obligated to add at the beginning of the meal. And likewise the reverse: if one began his meal on an ordinary day and continued his meal after the emergence of the stars on a day that is Rosh Ḥodesh, since he continued to eat a kezayit of bread after the emergence of the stars, he must add "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" in Birkat Ha-mazon.6

If Rosh Ḥodesh falls on Motza'ei Shabbat and one continued to eat a kezayit of bread after the emergence of the stars, the poskim disagree about what he should say in Birkat Ha-mazon: whether he should mention only Rosh Ḥodesh (Magen Avraham 188:18), or only Shabbat (Ben Ish Ḥai; Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:55), or mention both, because the time of the meal connects the two times (Taz 7; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 17). Some are accustomed to finish their meal before the emergence of the stars in order to avoid the doubt and mention "Retzei" alone. And according to my teacher and master, Rav Tzvi Yehuda Kook ztz"l, if one wishes to prolong his meal after the emergence of the stars and eats a kezayit of bread then, he should say "Retzei" and "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" (Olat Re'iya vol. 1, p. 364).

sections.title: One Who Forgot to Say Retzei or Ya'aleh Ve-yavo
sections.html:
The law for one who forgot to say "Retzei" or "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" in Birkat Ha-mazon depends on the obligation of the meal. If it is a meal at which it is obligatory to eat bread, it follows that he was obligated to recite Birkat Ha-mazon and to mention the day, and since he forgot, he must go back and recite Birkat Ha-mazon again. But if it is a meal at which there is no obligation to eat bread, he does not go back. Therefore, if he forgot to say "Retzei" at the first two meals of Shabbat, since he was obligated to eat bread at them, he must recite Birkat Ha-mazon again. But if he forgot to mention "Retzei" at Se'uda Shlishit, which after the fact can be fulfilled without bread, or if he forgot to say "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" on Rosh Ḥodesh or Ḥol Ha-mo'ed, on which there is no obligation to eat bread, he need not go back and recite Birkat Ha-mazon again (Berakhot 49b; SA 188:6-8; Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 7:6; Zemanim 1:11).

The same law applies to the two meals of Yom Tov, at which, according to most Rishonim, it is obligatory to eat bread; therefore, if he did not mention "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" at them, he must go back and recite Birkat Ha-mazon again, and this is the custom of most of Israel. Some have a different custom, as explained in the note.7

At meals for which one must go back, even if he has only begun the blessing of Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, he must go back to the beginning of Birkat Ha-mazon in order to say it properly. One should not make do with going back to the beginning of the blessing of "Raḥem," because once he has begun the blessing of Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, he is considered as one who has entirely finished the Torah blessings of Birkat Ha-mazon, and if he did not fulfill his obligation because he forgot to mention what he was obligated to mention, he must go back to their beginning (SA 188:6; BHL s.v. "la-rosh").

If he remembered that he forgot to say "Retzei" or "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" before he began the blessing of Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, the Sages instituted for him the wording of a supplementary blessing that he should say before beginning the blessing of Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. And even in a situation where the one who forgot is not obligated to repeat Birkat Ha-mazon, the Sages instituted saying the supplementary blessing. One who does not know the wording of the supplementary blessing does not fulfill his obligation by saying "Retzei" or "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" before the blessing of Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, and when the mention is indispensable, he should go back to the beginning (Taz; MB 17; and see BHL).8

When he forgot to say "Retzei" or "Ya'aleh Ve-yavo" and has already begun Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, and according to the law he need not repeat Birkat Ha-mazon, several poskim wrote that it is preferable that he mention what he forgot within the recitation of "Ha-raḥaman." Likewise, one who forgot to say "Al Ha-nissim," whose recitation is not indispensable, should properly say it within the recitation of "Ha-raḥaman," for there a person may add expressions of thanks as he wishes (Rema 682:1; MB 4; Peninei Halakha: Zemanim 11, note 7).

sections.title: Mayim Aḥaronim
sections.html:
The Sages said that it is obligatory to wash the hands before Birkat Ha-mazon, and this washing is called "mayim aḥaronim" ("final waters"). The reason for the washing is that they used Sodomite salt, which could blind the eyes (Ḥullin 105a-b). They further said that there is a mitzva to wash the hands before Birkat Ha-mazon in order to sanctify oneself for the blessing, for it is not fitting to say Birkat Ha-mazon when the hands are soiled with food remnants (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona and the Rosh, based on Berakhot 53b). And although it is obligatory to wash mayim aḥaronim, no blessing is recited over this washing, since the main purpose of the enactment is to prevent danger, and one does not recite a blessing over the removal of danger.

According to the Tosafists, there is no obligation today to wash mayim aḥaronim, because we do not use salt that endangers the eyesight. Furthermore, several of the great Aḥaronim wrote that there is not even a mitzva in it, because today, when we eat with cutlery, the hands do not become soiled from the food, and therefore there is no need to clean them in preparation for Birkat Ha-mazon.

In practice, although the view of most poskim is that even in our times one must wash mayim aḥaronim, many are accustomed to be lenient, among them Torah scholars and righteous women. This is because the law of mayim aḥaronim is rabbinic, and the rule is that in a dispute concerning a rabbinic law, the halakha follows the lenient view. However, one whose hands are soiled and who intends to rinse them anyway should rinse them before Birkat Ha-mazon (SA 181:1, 10).

The Kabbalists added a reason according to the esoteric teaching: through mayim aḥaronim one removes the impurity of the food that has stuck to the hands, which is the portion of the sitra aḥra (the "other side," the forces of impurity), and by removing it a person is protected from accusation (Zohar vol. 2, 154b; Zohar Ḥadash, Rut 106b). Therefore those who conduct themselves according to Kabbala are meticulous about washing mayim aḥaronim, but women did not adopt this Kabbalistic custom, and therefore in many families only the men are meticulous about washing mayim aḥaronim.9

sections.title: Laws of Mayim Aḥaronim
sections.html:
For those who are accustomed to wash mayim aḥaronim, one need wash only two joints of the fingers, and for the thumb one joint suffices, because the dirt of the food does not reach beyond that (SA 181:4). Some are meticulous to wash the entire fingers (BHL s.v. "ad"; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 15-16).

None of the laws that are indispensable for the washing before the meal apply to washing mayim aḥaronim; therefore there is no need to wash the hands from a vessel, but one may pour water over them directly from the tap, and many are accustomed to wash their hands from the tap into the sink. There is no minimum measure of water; the main thing is that the dirt be cleaned from the two joints of the fingers.10

One should not wash with very hot water, because when one washes with a little water, as people are accustomed to, it makes the dirt absorb into the hands (see SA 181:3).

When washing, one must lower the fingers, so that the water will run down and remove the dirt from the fingers (Sota 4b; SA 181:5). It is proper to dry the fingers before beginning to bless (SA 181:8; MB 19).

Mayim aḥaronim are not washed onto the ground, because the Sages said that they contain an evil spirit that can cause harm. Therefore, when one does not wash them into a sink, one must wash them into a vessel, and afterward pour the water into a sink or a place where people do not walk. It is customary, ideally, to remove the vessel from the table or to cover it before the blessing.11

After washing mayim aḥaronim, one should hasten to recite Birkat Ha-mazon, for the Sages said (Berakhot 42a): "Immediately following the washing of the hands comes the blessing." Ideally, one should not interrupt by speaking, even with words of Torah, between the washing and the blessing. Nor should one needlessly walk more than the distance of 22 amot, or pause in silence for the length of time it takes to walk 22 amot (see MB 179:1-2, BHL there, and 181:15 and 24).

sections.title: Customs in Birkat Ha-mazon
sections.html:
It is proper not to remove the tablecloth and the bread from the table until after Birkat Ha-mazon, for by leaving bread on the table one shows that God has given food in abundance, and thereby the thanks and praise in the blessing are said in completeness. In addition, a person should delay clearing away the bread, so that if a poor person happens to come to him, he will be able to break off some of his bread for him. The Sages said that whoever does not leave bread on his table at the time of the blessing does not see a sign of blessing. But if he prepares himself to give of his bread to the poor, God too will continue to grant him of His kindness. In addition, when a person leaves over some of his bread, he shows that he is happy with his lot and is even prepared to make do with less than what God has given him, and such a person is worthy of blessing. But if he finishes everything, it implies that he is not happy with his lot, and whatever he is given he will finish and will still want to eat more, and such a man is not worthy of blessing.

If they finished all the bread at the meal, it is good to bring bread to lie on the table at the time of the blessing. But if bread remains there, they should not bring more bread, because this is how the gentiles were accustomed to place bread after their meal in honor of their idolatry. It is preferable that from the outset there be plenty of bread on the table, so that some of it will remain until after the blessing (SA 180:1-2; Taz 1; MB 5).

One who eats away from home, and if he leaves remnants of bread he will later have to throw them away, should leave over only small crumbs, which fall anyway while he eats, and he should not eat them, so that he will see himself as having eaten and left over.12

In addition to the bread, it is customary to leave the salt on the table at the time of the blessing as well; however, regarding the remnants of other foods and the dirty dishes, there is no halakha. Some are meticulous to remove them from the table, so that the table will be clean in honor of Birkat Ha-mazon (Levush; and see Ben Ish Ḥai, Shelaḥ 2).

Several of the Rishonim wrote that it is customary to cover the sharp knife or to remove it from the table at the time of Birkat Ha-mazon. For the table resembles the altar, as the Sages said (Ḥagiga 27a) that now that a person has no altar on which to offer sacrifices to atone for his soul, his table, at which he hosts guests and the poor, atones for him. And just as we were commanded not to wield a sword over the stones of the altar (Shemot 20:22), because it is not fitting to wield the sword, which shortens a person's days, over the altar, which lengthens a person's days, so it is not fitting to place a sharp knife, which can shorten a person's days, on the table that is meant to add life, upon which we eat and bless. This custom was observed specifically at the time of the blessing, which is a time of kindness, whereas the knife alludes to judgment. However, on Shabbat and Yom Tov many are not particular about this, because they are days of holiness and blessing, and there is no need to be concerned on them about a bad sign (see BY, SA 180:5; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 6).

sections.title: The Manner of Reciting Birkat Ha-mazon and Its Dignity
sections.html:
One must sit at the time of the blessing, for this makes it easier to concentrate. Even one who was eating while standing or while walking about his house must sit for Birkat Ha-mazon. He should not recline in a manner of arrogance and levity, but rather sit in a dignified manner. After the fact, if he blessed while standing, walking or reclining, he has fulfilled his obligation (SA 183:9).

Some are meticulous to wear a jacket and put on a hat in honor of Birkat Ha-mazon (MB 183:11). But for one who is not accustomed to go about in a jacket and hat, there is no enhancement of the mitzva in this.

It is forbidden for a person to do work at the time of the blessing, even a slight action such as arranging the plate in front of him, so that he will not divert his attention from the blessing. In addition, one who busies himself with his hands during the blessing shows that he is not concentrating, harms the honor of Heaven and disgraces the blessing (SA 183:12; 191:3).

All the more so it is forbidden to interrupt by speaking in the middle of Birkat Ha-mazon. Some say that one who deliberately interrupts by speaking in the middle of Birkat Ha-mazon has lost all that he said and must begin Birkat Ha-mazon again from the beginning (Magen Avraham). However, in practice, after the fact, if he interrupted by speaking in the middle of Birkat Ha-mazon, he should continue from where he stopped and finish the blessing (MB 183:25).

Likewise, it is forbidden for a person to signal something to his friend at the time of the blessing, and if there is something there that disturbs his concentration, he should stop blessing and signal to his friend to remove it. And if a Torah scholar enters, it is permitted to rise in his honor.13

One who was eating while walking because he was hurrying on his way may also recite Birkat Ha-mazon while walking, because if he stops he will be preoccupied with the loss of time and will not be able to concentrate properly (SA 183:11; MB 36). Likewise one who is driving a car, if he is an experienced driver who is not preoccupied by the road, may in case of need bless while driving (see Sha'arei Teshuva 63:4). And the other passengers in the vehicle may bless ideally during the journey.

sections.title: Blessing in the Place Where One Ate (Which Foods Require a Blessing in Their Place)
sections.html:
Because of the importance of Birkat Ha-mazon, the Sages established that it be said in the place of the meal. Ideally, one should bless in the place where one sat while eating, and in case of need, as long as he is in the same room, he is considered as blessing in the place where he ate.14 Ideally, it is forbidden for a person to leave the place of his meal before reciting Birkat Ha-mazon, even if he intends to return.

If he forgot to bless and went on his way, or mistakenly thought that one may bless in another place, even if he traveled a great distance, he must return to the place of his meal in order to recite Birkat Ha-mazon. If he has a little bread where he is, instead of returning to the place of his meal he may wash his hands, recite Ha-motzi and eat a little of the bread, and afterward recite Birkat Ha-mazon; since he ate bread there too, it turns out that he blessed in the place where he ate. In a pressing situation, when he has no bread there and it is very difficult for him to return to the place of his meal, it is permitted to bless not in the place of eating (SA 184:1-2).15

Some say that only bread requires a blessing in its place (Rashba). According to many, all five species of grain require a blessing in their place, for whoever is obligated in the blessing of Al Ha-miḥya is obligated to recite it in the place where he ate (Rif, Tosafot and the Rosh). And some are stringent regarding all seven species, that whoever is obligated in the Me'ein Shalosh blessing must recite it in the place where he ate (Rambam).

Ideally, the blessing of Borei Nefashot too should be recited in the place of eating, for if he leaves there is a concern that he will forget to bless (MB 178:36). But if he left, he need not return, and likewise one who is in a hurry to leave may recite Borei Nefashot in another place. But with the seven species, and especially with the five species of grain, it is proper, when possible, to be stringent and return, in order to recite the after-blessing in the place where he ate.16

sections.title: Until When One May Bless
sections.html:
It is permitted to hold a meal for many hours, to pause between one course and the next for words of Torah and conversation, to sing and dance and continue eating, for as long as he still intends to continue his meal, the first blessing covers what he is about to eat, and Birkat Ha-mazon will cover all that he ate. Ideally, in order to maintain the continuity of the meal, it is preferable that 72 minutes not pass in which he neither eats nor drinks.

After he finishes his meal, he should hasten to recite Birkat Ha-mazon and not occupy himself with anything else before he blesses.

After the fact, if he did not bless immediately, he may bless as long as the enjoyment of what he ate continues, that is, as long as he still feels satiated from what he ate. If he became hungry, to the point that he began to want to eat another meal, he has lost the blessing. Generally, people do not feel hungry after a meal for several hours. If he ate light foods at the meal, the feeling of satiety lasts about two or three hours, and if he ate heavy foods, he will feel satiated for up to six hours. If he forgot to bless after the meal, and several hours have passed, and he is in doubt whether he has begun to be hungry, he should recite Birkat Ha-mazon, for since he was initially satisfied and became obligated in Birkat Ha-mazon by Torah law, in a situation of doubt he is obligated to bless. When it is clear to him that he has begun to be hungry again, or that six hours have passed, he has lost Birkat Ha-mazon.

If he ate a little bread and was not satisfied, as long as he still enjoys what he ate, that is, he still feels more satiated than he was before he began to eat, he may still recite Birkat Ha-mazon. This is difficult to estimate, and therefore a person who ate less than enough to be satisfied must hasten to bless immediately after finishing eating. After the fact, if about an hour has passed without his having blessed, ideally he should eat another kezayit, and in this way he will be able to recite Birkat Ha-mazon according to all views. If he does not have another kezayit there, as long as 72 minutes have not passed since he finished eating, he may still bless, and after that he should not bless. Only if it is clear to him that he is still more satiated than he was before he ate may he bless even after 72 minutes.17
